criteria.name: in_app_diagnosis_md_does_the_note_iden
criteria.description: In /app/diagnosis.md, does the note identify that the flow-controlled push consumer delivers a message before replicating its delivered state, so that after a consumer leadership change a delivery issued before the change can still arrive after it?
criteria.reasoning: The note says the flow-control exception sends the message to outq immediately after proposing updateDeliveredOp, without waiting for quorum. It also says a delivery issued by the old leader can still be in flight and arrive after the new leader restores state. Its worked interleaving has the old leader's upstream 552 / delivery 552 arriving after the leadership change. That matches the criterion's two points: delivery happens before the delivered state is replicated, and a pre-change delivery can arrive after the change.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_state_that_after
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md state that after the consumer is reset its delivery sequence restarts at 1, so a stale delivery from before the reset can take the delivery number a new delivery needs?
criteria.reasoning: The submission's diagnosis centers on uncommitted delivery numbers being reused after a leadership change. It also describes a second race, where selection continues during a pending reset and entries carry the old epoch's delivery numbers. It never says that a reset restarts the delivery sequence at 1, so a stale pre-reset delivery can take the number a new delivery needs. It mentions that reset establishes "next delivery number 1" only as part of the repair. Its main mechanism is reuse of the restored delivered state's next number after a leader change, not a restart at 1 after a reset. The stale-delivery-collides-with-new-delivery idea is partly present, but the specific claim about the reset restarting at 1 is missing as a cause.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_the_downs
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain the downstream consequence: the source drops the new message as a duplicate and the mirror marks its sequence deleted, leaving interior gaps the origin still holds?
criteria.reasoning: The submission explains the downstream consequence. A reused delivery number makes the receiver treat the new message as a duplicate. The duplicate is suppressed, but it still advances delivery accounting. The mirror then calls skipMsgs and marks the sequence as skipped or deleted. Later arrival of the missing message is suppressed because it is older than the watermark. The result is interior holes while the origin retains everything, with no error logged and the stream still progressing. Its mechanism differs from the reference's. It uses a stale or duplicate message advancing the count, and a later message being dropped as old. The reference has the new message dropped as a duplicate. Even so, the key consequence is covered: the new message is dropped, the mirror marks the sequence deleted, and interior gaps remain that the origin still holds. The source's behavior is described somewhat differently, because it accepts the jump rather than marking deletes. That is a minor difference.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_rule_out_ordinary
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md rule out ordinary message redelivery as the cause, on the grounds that the messages are lost rather than re-sent?
criteria.reasoning: The diagnosis says "Ordinary redelivery is not itself data loss": a retry can raise the consumer delivery sequence without raising the stream sequence, and "repeated delivery of an origin message does not delete an interior downstream message." It also says the loss is interior holes while the origin stays intact. That rules out ordinary redelivery as the cause. The reasoning is framed a little differently from the reference's "lost rather than re-sent". It still says redelivery re-sends and does not remove data, so it matches in substance. It does allow redelivery to take part in the bad interleaving, but it rejects redelivery as the root cause.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_rule_out_legitima
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md rule out legitimate duplicate suppression as the cause, recognising that a genuinely new message is being misclassified as a duplicate?
criteria.reasoning: The diagnosis says ordinary duplicate suppression is not itself data loss. It says the defect makes delivery accounting give false evidence of continuity. It says a late missing message is suppressed only as a consequence of that false continuity decision. It also says the receiver's continuity test is passed by reused delivery numbers, so a genuinely new upstream message (such as 551) is wrongly suppressed after the watermark has advanced. This is the same conclusion as the reference, which reads it as a new message misclassified as a duplicate. The mechanism differs a little, but the ruling-out is explicit.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_rule_out_acknowle
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md rule out acknowledgement lag as the cause, noting that lag does not delete interior sequences or lose messages permanently?
criteria.reasoning: The diagnosis has a bullet, "Ordinary acknowledgement lag is not itself data loss." It says ack state may trail delivered state, causing pending messages and retries. It says this "does not authorize skipping retained origin data." It says faster acknowledgements or waiting for lag to clear is "no correctness fix." That rules out ack lag as the cause. It conveys that lag does not permanently lose messages. It does not say in those exact words that lag doesn't delete interior sequences, but the point comes through. Other parts of the document add that the missing data is an interior hole caused by false continuity. This is close enough to the criterion.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_justify_that_deli
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md justify that deliveries must be held while a reset is pending, because a delivery proposed before the reset applies must not mix into the delivered state after it?
criteria.reasoning: The diagnosis argues that a reset must act as a barrier for delivery selection. It says getNextMsg returns errConsumerReset while a reset is pending. It says a delivery selected before the reset and reaching quorum during the barrier is released without being sent. It says a generation value invalidates messages prepared before the reset, so stale old-epoch delivery numbers can't follow the reset entry. This matches the reasoning that a delivery proposed before the reset applies must not mix into the delivered state after it. The explanation is framed around selection and in-flight entries carrying old-epoch delivery numbers, not the exact wording, but it justifies the same thing.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_how_afte
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain how, after a reset, the downstream agrees with the consumer on which delivery number comes next, and why that agreement must hold even when delivery resumes before the post-reset state is gathered? An equivalent mechanism of the submitted repair counts.
criteria.reasoning: The criterion asks the doc to explain how, after a reset, the downstream agrees with the consumer on the next delivery number. The reference does this by having the reset response report the reset point and having the downstream seed its delivery counting from it. The reason given is that delivery resumes before post-reset consumer info is gathered. The submission never describes that mechanism or an equivalent. It handles the problem on the producer side. It blocks selection during a reset, uses a quorum delivery path, applies a generation guard, and resets the consumer's own state to sequence `seq` and delivery 1. It does not say that the downstream is told or seeded with the post-reset delivery number. It also does not explain why that agreement must hold when delivery resumes before info is gathered. The submission's stated principle is that the producer enforces the existing continuity assumptions, so there is no downstream-consumer agreement mechanism. It does not meet the criterion.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_how_its_r
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain how its repair keeps a delivery that arrives after a reset, carrying a stale or reused delivery number, from being counted as a new delivery?
criteria.reasoning: The criterion asks whether the diagnosis explains how the repair keeps a post-reset delivery carrying a stale or reused delivery number from being counted as new. The submission does this, though by a different mechanism from the reference. It does not change the receiver's counting. Instead it stops reuse at the producer. Delivery numbers are made durable by quorum before they become visible. A reset barrier blocks selection while a reset is pending. A generation value invalidates messages prepared before a reset. Queued pre-reset deliveries are released without being sent. Flow-control identity and byte accounting are cleared so delayed old responses cannot cross a reset. The submission also states that stale deliveries are suppressed as duplicates, and that the repair enforces the receiver's continuity assumptions at the producer. This covers stale or reused delivery numbers after a reset, so it qualifies.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_how_its_r
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain how its repair keeps a genuinely new message from being dropped as a duplicate when a stale delivery has already taken its delivery number?
criteria.reasoning:
The criterion asks whether the diagnosis explains how the repair keeps a genuinely new message from being dropped as a duplicate when a stale delivery has already taken its delivery number. The reference does this by counting each delivery once: it tracks the last counted stream sequence and advances only when the delivery number is one past the last and the stream sequence is above the last counted. A new source message whose delivery number is not above the last counted is retried instead of dropped.

The submission takes a different approach. Its repair works at the producer. It sends deliveries only after quorum, adds a reset barrier, and uses a generation value to invalidate stale deliveries. It states that it does not change the receiver. It says "Only changing mirror gap detection would break legitimate upstream deletion..." and "These changes preserve the protocol's existing continuity assumptions by enforcing them at the producer."

The submission does explain how a stale delivery that takes a delivery number leads to the loss of a new message. It also explains how its producer-side repair prevents delivery numbers from being reused. But it never explains how the repair stops a genuinely new message from being dropped as a duplicate once a stale delivery has already taken its number. It prevents the stale delivery from occurring at all, and it does not handle the case where one has already happened.

The match is therefore only loose, and the specific mechanism the criterion asks about is missing.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_why_repai
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain why repairing only the consumer side, or only the downstream accounting, leaves the defect in place?
criteria.reasoning: The diagnosis explicitly explains why a narrow fix fails. It says changing only mirror gap detection would break legitimate deletion handling and would not make the consumer numbering trustworthy. It also says that fixing only the producer side, such as removing the flow-control exception, would leave the reset-era selection race. The same section covers delaying flow-control packets or clearing byte accounting alone, and a pending-reset check done only at send time. This matches the criterion, though the reference's consumer-plus-stream split is framed differently. Here the downstream fix is argued against rather than combined with a consumer fix.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_why_resta
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain why restarting the servers does not fix it (the defect is in delivery/reset accounting, not transient runtime state)?
criteria.reasoning: The "Restarting servers" section explains that a restart restores persisted/agreed state, doesn't undo downstream skip records or watermarks, and leaves the faulty delivery path in the binary. It adds that a restart can itself expose the discrepancy and that a quiet restart might only avoid the race on one run. This locates the defect in delivery/reset accounting and not in transient runtime state, which is what the criterion asks for.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_why_purgi
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain why purging/truncating/re-reading a downstream stream, or deleting and recreating the consumer, mirror or source, does not fix it?
criteria.reasoning: The diagnosis has a section, "Why operational shortcuts are not repairs". It covers purging/truncating/re-reading downstream. Purging destroys stored messages. Re-reading doesn't fill holes because of the watermark. Neither prevents recurrence at the next transition. It also covers deleting and recreating the consumer, mirror and source. That discards state, leaves the defect in place so it can recur, and doesn't clear the watermark. This matches the reference's reasoning: it destroys stored messages and the race recurs.

criteria.name: does_app_diagnosis_md_explain_why_turni
criteria.description: Does /app/diagnosis.md explain why turning off flow control on the consumer does not fix it (the race is independent of flow control, which must stay active)?
criteria.reasoning: The "Turning off consumer flow control" section says AckFlowControl requires flow control, so disabling it isn't permitted. It also says "disabling flow control does not repair the reset barrier and is not a repair of the required durable flow-controlled path. The corrected path keeps flow control enabled." This covers both that the reset race is independent of flow control and that flow control must stay active. The document also describes the flow-control exception as part of the cause, which is a bit at odds with the reference. The explanation still covers both required points, though it is brief.

guard.reasoning: The document is a technical diagnosis and it does not address the evaluator or discuss how its work should be scored. The test results, the validation notes and the statements about what was and wasn't changed are all engineering reporting. For example, "No test code or history setting was changed to accommodate it" describes the work and isn't aimed at a grader.
